name: Plank
tierNote: Safety tier C (content.md 5.1: not in the A or B lists); census.json difficulty tier 2.

claims.text: Start lying face down, elbows close to the sides and directly under the shoulders, palms down, hands facing forward.

quotes.text: Lie prone (on your stomach) on an exercise mat or floor with your elbows close to your sides and directly under your shoulders, palms down and hands facing forward.

claims.text: Before lifting, tense the thighs to straighten the legs, pull the toes toward the shins and brace the trunk.

quotes.text: Contract your quadriceps to extend your legs and dorsiflex your ankles (pull toes towards your shins). Contract your core and abdominal muscles to stiffen your torso.

claims.text: Lift the whole body slowly, keeping trunk and legs stiff.

quotes.text: Slowly lift your entire torso off the floor or mat, maintaining a stiff torso and legs.

claims.text: In the hold, avoid a sagging low back, hips hiked up, or bent knees.

quotes.text: Avoid any arching (sagging) in your low back, hiking (upwards) in your hips or bending in the knees.

claims.text: Keep the shoulders directly over the elbows and don't shrug.

quotes.text: Avoid shrugging your shoulder and keep your shoulders positioned directly over your elbows with your palms facing down.

claims.text: Keep breathing through the hold, held for a set time of 5 seconds or more.

quotes.text: Continue to breath while holding this position for a specified time (5+ seconds).

claims.text: Lower back down with the trunk stiff and knees straight, then relax.

quotes.text: While maintaining a stiff torso and extended knees, gently lower your body back towards the mat or floor before relaxing.

claims.text: Low-back pain during the plank means stop.

quotes.text: If you experience any pain in the low back with this movement, stop the exercise immediately and consult with your doctor.

claims.text: In 30-second holds, a long-lever plank with a backward (posterior) pelvic tilt raised abdominal muscle activity versus the traditional prone plank; the long lever tends to contribute more than the tilt, and the tilt alone raised external-oblique activity.

quotes.text: Nineteen participants performed all four variations of the plank for 30 seconds in a randomized order
while the posterior tilt plank elicited greater activity in the external oblique (p = 0.028)

In conclusion, the long-lever posterior-tilt plank significantly increases muscle activation compared to the traditional prone plank. The long-lever component tends to contribute more to these differences than the posterior-tilt component.

claims.text: Plank EMG studies record the rectus abdominis and the obliques (with the erector spinae) as working muscles.

quotes.text: the long-lever posterior-tilt plank displayed a significantly increased activation of the upper rectus abdominis (p < 0.001), lower abdominal stabilizers (p < 0.001), and external oblique (p < 0.001).
Surface EMG of the rectus abdominis (RA), external oblique (EO), internal oblique (IO), and erector spinae (ES) was collected in 15 participants

claims.text: Of four prone-plank versions, a backward (posterior) pelvic tilt with the shoulder blades drawn together (scapular adduction) gave more overall EMG activity than the two forward-tilt versions, and was rated the hardest of the four.

quotes.text: Four variations of the prone plank were evaluated: scapular abduction with anterior (ABANT) and posterior (ABRET) pelvic tilt; and scapular adduction with anterior (ADANT), and posterior (ADRET) pelvic tilt.
The ADRET resulted in higher overall EMG activity compared with ABANT (p = 0.04) and ADANT (p = 0.04).
Finally, ADRET provoked a higher RPE compared with ABANT (p = 0.000), ABRET (p = 0.001), and ADANT (p = 0.015).

claims.text: Front plank: 1–6 reps of a 10–60 second hold, resting 30–60 seconds between reps; build up from a few seconds (3, then 4, then 10), with a full minute as the goal.

quotes.text: Front plank Reps: 1–6 Sets: 1 Hold: 10–60 seconds Rest: 30–60 seconds between reps
quotes.where: Core strength exercises: Planks, Front plank

quotes.text: "If you can hold it for three seconds, try it for four. If you can hold it for four, try to get to 10 seconds," says Dr. Edward Phillips, assistant professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation at Harvard Medical School.
The ultimate goal is to be able to hold your plank for a full minute.

claims.text: Plank tips: keep the neck and spine neutral, keep the shoulders down and back, and don't bend at the hips.

quotes.text: Keep your neck and spine neutral during the plank.
quotes.where: Core strength exercises: Planks, Plank tips and techniques

quotes.text: Keep your shoulders down and back.
quotes.where: Core strength exercises: Planks, Plank tips and techniques

quotes.text: Don't bend at your hips.
quotes.where: Core strength exercises: Planks, Plank tips and techniques

claims.text: If you cannot hold the plank, rest on the knees instead of the feet.

quotes.text: If you can't hold the position, modify the exercise by resting your weight on your knees instead of your feet (sometimes referred to as a modified push-up position).

plate.viewWhy: The faults ACE names (sagging low back, hiked hips, bent knees, shoulders not over elbows; c4, c5) are all a line from the side.
plate.frames: Hold convention (architecture section 1): entry pose (lying face down, c1) then the held pose; Trace follows the path into the hold.
plate.start: Entry: face down, forearms on the floor, elbows under the shoulders, palms down (c1); legs straight, toes pulled up (c2).
plate.end: Held pose: body lifted onto forearms and toes, straight line from shoulders through hips to heels, knees straight (c3, c4), shoulders over elbows (c5).

checkpoints.label: Elbows under shoulders
checkpoints.what: Shoulders stacked over the elbows, no shrug.

checkpoints.label: Hips level
checkpoints.what: No sagging low back and no hiked hips.

checkpoints.label: Knees straight
checkpoints.what: Legs straight and stiff through the hold.

mistake.why: ACE and Harvard both tell the lifter to avoid it (c4, c13).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 3: hips hiked up (c4, c13), by step 3's count. Step 1 finds no frequency word for a fault: Harvard's 'Common Conditions' is a site menu and "sometimes referred to as a modified push-up position" names a version; "doing as many reps as needed" is about reps; Cortell's "Prone plank is a widely used exercise in core stability training." is about the exercise; Schoenfeld's "tends to contribute more" is about muscle activity (and 'tend' is not a frequency word). ACE has none. Step 2 finds no named fault tied to harm: ACE's "If you experience any pain in the low back with this movement, stop the exercise immediately and consult with your doctor." (c8) names pain but no fault; Harvard's "There's a saying that when you can hold a plank for a minute, your back pain will be gone," and "Planks may ease back pain because as your core muscles strengthen, they provide more support for your spine." are benefits, and 'A lumbar belt may help ease low back pain', 'Light exposure at night may raise risk for heart disease', 'Whole grains may improve several heart risk factors at once' and the 'Related Topics' pain links are page chrome linking other articles; none names a plank fault. Step 3: no read source has a common-mistakes list (Harvard's 'Plank tips and techniques' is a tips list), so the count decides (D-SUP-LB6-CCP): the read sources that tell the lifter to avoid each fault (sources, not lists). Hips hiked 2: ACE "hiking (upwards) in your hips" (c4) and Harvard "Don't bend at your hips." (c13), read as hip bending, the hips piking up. Low back sagging 1: ACE "Avoid any arching (sagging) in your low back" (c4). Knees bending 1: ACE (c4). Shrugging 1: ACE "Avoid shrugging your shoulder" (c5). Not counted, as they only give the right position: Harvard's "Keep your neck and spine neutral during the plank." and "Keep your shoulders down and back." (c13), "Be certain to keep your back straight and your head in a neutral position looking at the ground." and "aligning your shoulders directly over your elbows"; ACE's "keep your shoulders positioned directly over your elbows" (c5) and "Continue to breath while holding this position" (c6). Schoenfeld and Cortell name no fault. So LR-31's top fault is the hips hiked up, and drawable is true (the side view shows the hips raised above the shoulder-heel line). Harvard's line counts for the hiked hips, as hiking the hips is bending at the hips (D-SUP-LB9-PLANK). Pilot A: the pick went to the owner sheet as plank-R1 (D-SUP-LB8-PILOTS, R-LB9-3) and is applied (D-SUP-LB9-PLANK, D-LIB8M-ROUTED), so plate.mistake and handlingMistakes[0] are the hiked hips; the sag is handlingMistakes[1]. The head's old note, "ACE lists sagging first", is not an LR-31 step (ACE's sentence is an avoid line, not a common-mistakes list).

tempo.text: Hold 10–60 seconds, 1–6 reps, rest 30–60 seconds (c12); beginners build up from a few seconds toward a full minute (c12). ACE: at least 5 seconds while breathing (c6).

grip.handContact: Forearms and palms flat on the floor, hands facing forward.
grip.note: Hand archetype none (forearm plank): no hand zoom.

setup.step: Lie face down, elbows under your shoulders, palms down.
Straighten your legs, pull your toes up, brace your trunk.
Lift slowly, trunk and legs stiff.
Hold for the set time and keep breathing.
Lower back down with the body still stiff.

posture.point: Low back does not sag; hips not hiked.
Harder version: tilt the pelvis backward and draw the shoulder blades together.

handlingMistakes.fix: Brace your trunk. Can't hold it? Rest on your knees.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Shrugging, shoulders drifting away from the elbows.

rows.where: Front and sides of the belly

risks.risk: Low back sagging (arching) during the hold.
Low-back pain during the hold: stop.

zooms.right: No sagging low back, no hiked hips.

zooms.wrong: Shoulders shrugged, not over the elbows.

libraryDiff.why: Add obliques as secondary: both EMG studies measure oblique activity during the prone plank (c10). Library keeps core primary, abs secondary, glutes and front_delts as stabilizers (no source found for or against those two).
